&l;p&g;&l;img class=&q;dam-image getty size-large wp-image-930289338&q; src=&q;https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/930289338/960×0.jpg?fit=scale&q; data-height=&q;640&q; data-width=&q;960&q;&g;&q;Look at Trump&s;s funny tweet. He said he was going to kick our mothers or something like this.&q;&a;nbsp; (Photo&a;nbsp;by&a;nbsp; NICOLAS ASFOURI/AFP/Getty Images)
The Chinese economy has been resilient up to now. But the trade war is only just beginning.&a;nbsp; By the end of the summer, investors will have a better sense of how big this bang gets. For now, only $34 billion in products have tariffs, with another $16 billion or so expected before the end of the month. Come September, another $200 billion worth of Made in China goods could be subject to tariffs of roughly 10%.&a;nbsp; How does China cope with that?
For some, China should just boycott American brands. For others, they should nail American multinationals that have grown dependent on China for revenue. Think Apple, for instance. If the $200 billion in new tariffs becomes a reality, going after certain multinationals is more likely than boycotting American brands. American brands are important to China&s;s two new favorite companies, Alibaba and Tencent, both run by new tech billionaires, Jack Ma and &s;Pony&s; Ma. Boycotting Nikes won&s;t make the Ma boys happy, and these two are the faces of new, tech-savvy&a;nbsp;China. Unlikely that Xi Jinping punishes Alibaba and Tencent consumers because of Trump&s;s trade policy.
&l;p class=&q;tweet_line&q;&g;Domestic growth momentum is slowing and a negative trade war effect is expected in the coming months.&a;nbsp; To alleviate the impact, monetary and fiscal policy will likely be adjusted sooner rather than later in an effort to offset any negative external shock and to stabilize growth. That means lower interest rates, tax breaks and maybe other forms of credit stimulus. Indeed some tax breaks have already been announced on the individual level.
&l;p class=&q;tweet_line&q;&g;The upcoming July meeting of&a;nbsp;the Communist Party leadership should offer more related signals, UBS says.&l;/p&g;
&q;Adjustments may include increased liquidity offerings; a more gradual approach to financial regulatory tightening; and funding for infrastructure projects,&q; UBS economists led by Donna Kwok wrote in a research note to clients dated July 16. Local bond issuance is also a possibility. That means more debt coming online in the months ahead. For investors worried about China&s;s debt profile, this could be perceived as another negative.
&l;strong&g;See: &l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/kenrapoza/2018/07/10/has-the-media-overinflated-the-risks-of-a-china-trade-war/#31d1061835fb&q;&g;Has The Media Overinflated The Risks Of A China Trade War?&l;/a&g;— Forbes&l;/strong&g;
&l;img class=&q;dam-image bloomberg size-large wp-image-42356520&q; src=&q;https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/42356520/960×0.jpg?fit=scale&q; data-height=&q;670&q; data-width=&q;960&q;&g; Jack Ma, billionaire and chairman of Alibaba Group. Boycotting American brands, as some have suggested, would be a negative for Ma. Alibaba&s;s share price is up only 4% YTD while its American counterpart, Amazon, is up over 55%. Negative sentiment on China hasn&s;t helped. Photographer: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Bloomberg
UBS does not think that China devalues the renminbi (RMB).
Competitive devaluation would also be a problem for China and its relationship with the International Monetary Fund. The RMB is now part of the IMFs Special Drawing Rights, a combination of world-leading currencies used to fund IMF loan packages. An RMB made weaker by purposeful devaluation would not go over well with the IMF. In order to be included in the SDR basket, countries have to adhere to market principals regarding their currencies.
&q;China will not intentionally use currency depreciation or sale of its U.S. Treasury holdings as tools to fight the trade war,&q; says Kwok. Dumping Treasury bonds was another possibility of China&s;s retaliatory measures. China is not expected to make any major moves in the U.S. bond market, but if the U.S. does hit China with more tariffs by the end of the summer, markets should expect some form of retaliation.
Because of all this uncertainty, the RMB is seen weakening due to&a;nbsp;the combination of a slower economy and less capital inflows from corporate and foreign portfolio investment.
UBS estimated recently that the 25% tariff on the scheduled $50 billion worth of China imports going into effect this month would reduce China&s;s GDP growth by a tiny 0.1% over the next 12 months.
Matthews Asia investment strategist Andy Rothman made a similar forecast in June, &l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/kenrapoza/2018/06/26/heres-how-the-bull-market-dies/#71eddf7f434f&q;&g;cited here on June 26&l;/a&g;.
Market consensus is for China growth to be 6.6% this year.&a;nbsp; But if more tariffs are placed on Chinese imports, the impact in the 12 months that follow their enactment could see as much as a half a percent trimmed off Chinese GDP, UBS economists believe.
